title: Early Childhood Intervention and Life-Cycle Skill Development: Evidence from Head Start
research_question: What are the long-term effects of participating in a federally funded preschool program for poor children on cognitive test scores, school-age outcomes (such as grade retention and learning disability diagnosis), and young adult outcomes (such as high school graduation, college attendance, idleness, crime, teen parenthood, and health)? How do short-term test score gains relate to longer-run benefits, and how do effects vary by race, gender, and maternal cognitive ability?
data_description: The primary data source is the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 Children and Young Adults (CNLSY), which since 1986 has biennially surveyed all children born to the 6,283 women in the NLSY 1979 cohort, through 2004. The unit of observation is the child (with multiple children per mother enabling within-family comparisons). Key variables include contemporaneously reported preschool participation (Head Start, other preschool, none), PPVT and PIAT Math and Reading Recognition test scores administered repeatedly from ages 5–14, grade retention, learning disability diagnosis, and young adult outcomes measured at age 19+ (high school graduation, GED, college attendance, idleness, self-reported crime, teen parenthood, self-reported health). Pre-treatment covariates include birth weight, maternal AFQT, permanent income, maternal education and work history, childcare arrangements, family structure, and infant health. The analysis sample covers children age four or older by 1990, with at least one age-eligible sibling, yielding 3,698 children (1,251 in the within-family sample). Most participants were enrolled in the program between 1984 and 1990.
institutional_context: Head Start is a federally funded, nationwide preschool program launched in 1965 as part of the War on Poverty, serving over 900,000 poor children annually with a budget of $6.8 billion. Funding rules require that 90 percent of participants be at or below the federal poverty line, on public assistance, or in foster care. The program is a 9-month, full- or part-day preschool costing roughly $7,000–$9,000 per child per year—about 60 percent of the cost of model programs such as Perry Preschool and Carolina Abecedarian. Beyond preschool education, it provides medical, dental, mental health, nutrition, and parenting services, emphasizing 'whole child' development rather than academic preparation. Programs are administered locally under federal quality guidelines, generating heterogeneity across sites. The program is chronically oversubscribed, with waiting lists, and enrollment is capped at two years (modal enrollment is one year). Public investment has more than tripled in real terms since inception, yet skepticism about its long-run value motivates renewed evaluation, particularly for cohorts enrolled in the late 1980s when alternative preschool options had expanded substantially.
